name: Dependency Inversion Principle
intent: Make the code that holds your business rules depend on abstractions that it owns, and make the code that talks to mail servers and databases depend on those same abstractions, so the details can change without touching the rules.
scenario: An order service places orders: it checks them, saves them and emails the customer. Two more services, invoices and reminders, send email in the same way. The first version creates its own SMTP mailer and SQL database. Then the company moves to another mail provider, and a developer wants to add one more test of the order rule.
problem: When a rule creates the mailer and the database itself, it is welded to them. A test of the rule needs a mail server and a database. Swapping the provider means opening every service that names the old class. And the code that decides how orders work, which changes for business reasons, is edited whenever a technical detail changes, so each of those edits can break a rule that was fine.

howItWorks.title: State the principle in two halves
howItWorks.text: High-level modules (the policy: what an order is, when it is valid) should not depend on low-level modules (SMTP, SQL, the file system). Both should depend on abstractions. And the abstractions should not depend on details: the details depend on the abstractions. The usual shorthand, depend on interfaces, leaves out the important part: who owns the interface.

howItWorks.title: Let the policy own the abstraction
howItWorks.text: The order service declares what it needs in its own words: a Notifier that tells a customer something, an OrderStore that saves an order. These interfaces live with the policy and are shaped by what the policy wants to say, not by what a mail library can do. Now the source-code arrow from the mailer points up at the policy's interface: the dependency that used to point down has been inverted.

howItWorks.title: Write adapters at the edge
howItWorks.text: The SMTP code and the SQL code implement the policy's interfaces. An adapter translates between what the policy asks (notify this customer) and what the library needs (host, port, MIME headers). When the provider changes, the adapter is rewritten and nothing above it is touched.

howItWorks.title: Hand the details in from outside
howItWorks.text: Something has to choose the real implementations. A composition root, usually the program's entry point, creates SmtpMailer and SqlDatabase and passes them to the services. This handing-in is dependency injection: a technique, and the usual way to build an inverted design. Tests do the same with fakes, so a rule is tested in memory, with no infrastructure.

howItWorks.title: Keep the three terms apart
howItWorks.text: Dependency inversion is a design principle: who owns the interface and which way source dependencies point. Dependency injection is a technique: dependencies are passed in rather than created inside. Inversion of control is a style in which a framework calls your code (a web framework calling your handler) instead of you calling it. You can inject without inverting (pass in a concrete class), and use inversion of control without either.

pros: Swapping a provider changes the adapter and the place that wires it, not the rules
Rules can be tested in memory with fakes, without a mail server or a database
The code that changes for business reasons is separated from the code that changes for technical ones
Details can be chosen late, or differ per environment, without a rewrite
cons: More files and one more hop to follow a call, which makes the code harder to read for a newcomer
A badly drawn abstraction leaks the detail it was meant to hide, and then the layer costs more than it saves
Wiring has to live somewhere, so a composition root (or a container) must be built and kept tidy
In a small, short-lived program the indirection may never pay back
whenToUse: Business rules that outlive the technology around them, or that must be tested fast and in isolation
A detail you expect to swap or fake: a mail or payment provider, a clock, a message broker
Code with several services that all talk to the same external system
whenNotToUse: Pure value types and stable helpers (a Money class, a string formatter), which have nothing to replace
Throwaway scripts and small tools where the detail will never change
Details that already have a stable standard interface you are happy to depend on directly, such as a file stream
pitfalls: An interface that mirrors a single implementation: it is named after the SMTP class and shaped by its methods, so nothing was inverted and any provider change still reaches the policy
Injecting concrete types and calling it DIP: the class receives SmtpMailer through its constructor, but still depends on the detail, so a swap now touches the constructors as well
A service locator: a class asks a global registry for its dependencies inside its methods. Dependencies become invisible, and a test fails at run time when something was not registered
Interfaces for everything, including value classes, clocks and pure helpers, which adds files and hops and gives nothing back
Putting the interface in the details' project, so the policy references the infrastructure assembly and the arrow still points down
Treating a DI container as the principle: containers are a convenience for wiring, and a codebase can invert dependencies with plain constructors

roles.label: Policy
roles.description: High-level code with the business rules, such as the order service.

roles.label: Abstraction
roles.description: An interface owned by the policy, in the policy's own words.

roles.label: Detail
roles.description: Low-level code that talks to a mail server or a database.

roles.label: Composition root
roles.description: The entry point that creates the details and passes them in.

roles.label: Test
roles.description: Checks a rule, ideally in memory with fakes.

quiz.question: A team defines IMailer in the infrastructure project, with Send(host, port, from, to, body), and SmtpMailer implements it. OrderService takes an IMailer in its constructor. The company moves to a provider with an API-key and template model. What happens?
options: Nothing in OrderService changes, because it only depends on an interface and not on a class.
OrderService is edited too, because the interface was shaped by SMTP and nothing was inverted.
Only the composition root changes, because injection hides the provider from every other class.
The tests change, but the production code does not, because interfaces are only used for tests.
quiz.explanation: An interface that mirrors one implementation carries the detail up with it: host and port are SMTP ideas, so a provider with templates does not fit and the policy has to change. Owning the interface means shaping it by what the policy needs, such as notify a customer. Injection alone does not invert anything.

quiz.question: Which sentence keeps dependency inversion, dependency injection and inversion of control apart correctly?
options: Dependency injection is a technique for handing dependencies in, and inversion is about who owns the interface.
Inversion of control is the formal name of the principle, and injection is just another word for it.
Dependency inversion means using a DI container, and inversion of control means avoiding one.
All three describe passing objects through constructors, and differ only in the framework used.
quiz.explanation: Inversion is a design principle about the direction of source dependencies. Injection is one technique that helps. Inversion of control is a separate idea in which a framework calls your code. You can inject a concrete class and invert nothing.

quiz.question: A service calls Registry.Get<INotifier>() inside its Place method. The interface is owned by the policy. What is the main cost compared with a constructor parameter?
options: The interface is no longer owned by the policy, so the dependency arrow points down again.
The registry makes the code slower, since every call must search a global list of types.
The class has hidden dependencies, and a test fails at run time if nothing was registered.
A registry cannot return fakes, so the service cannot be tested without real infrastructure.
quiz.explanation: A locator keeps the abstraction but hides what a class needs: the constructor no longer says so, and a missing registration shows up as a failure at run time. Speed is rarely the issue, and a registry can return fakes, so the cost is visibility, not ownership.
